--- title: "What one row is" description: "Observations, features, responses and labels, plus the question marine data makes genuinely hard: how many independent observations do you actually have?" order: 1 categories: [data-preparation, marine-data] --- ## The rectangle and what it hides Machine learning wants a rectangle: rows of observations, columns of variables, one column singled out as the thing to predict. Getting your data into that shape looks clerical. It is not. The choice of what a row represents fixes what the model can learn, what "independent" means, and, as we will see, how much data you actually have, which is usually less than the row count suggests. This is also where marine data stops resembling the textbook. A trawl, a CTD cast, a photograph, a fish, a monitoring site: any of them could be "one observation", and they give different answers. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. The R tab is what produced the tables and figures you see; the Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent, shown for translation rather than executed by the site. Figures stay in R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. It is real code, not pseudocode: it runs against the same files through `python/mlbasic_data.py`, and `python/check-snippets.py` executes every snippet in the site to keep it honest. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly**: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## The idea ### The vocabulary, and its synonyms Machine learning grew up in computer science and statistics separately, so the same thing has two or three names. Reading across literatures is much easier once you have the map. | In this course | Also called | What it is | | --- | --- | --- | | **Observation** | row, instance, example, sample, case | One thing you measured | | **Feature** | predictor, covariate, independent variable, input, attribute | Something you know about it | | **Response** | outcome, target, dependent variable, $y$ | The thing you want the model to produce | | **Label** | class, annotation, ground truth | The response when it is a category, usually assigned by a person | Two notes on the traps in that table. "Sample" means a single observation in machine learning and the whole collection of them in field science, so be careful which you mean in a mixed-discipline meeting. And "ground truth" is a confident phrase for something that is usually one specialist's opinion; [section 7](../07-validation/index.qmd) returns to the fact that your labels have an error rate too. ### The harder question The vocabulary is easy. This is not: > **What is one observation?** Consider a survey that visits 160 monitoring sites, several times each, over six years. A row could reasonably be: - **one trawl**: what the database stores; - **one site-year**: if you average the trawls, because repeat trawls at a site on the same day are not independent; - **one site**: if the site's character, not the visit, is what varies; - **one fish**: if you are modelling individual growth rather than abundance. There is no universally right answer. There is an answer that matches your scientific question, and the cost of getting it wrong is that your model, and every confidence interval and cross-validation score attached to it, silently treats correlated rows as independent evidence. ## Worked example Here is the survey as it came off the ship, rather than the tidy extract used in [section 1](../01-introduction/index.qmd). ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} raw <- load_coastal_survey_raw() dim(raw) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] 815 17 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} names(raw) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] "station_id" "site_id" "vessel" #> [4] "sample_date" "survey_year" "season" #> [7] "longitude" "latitude" "depth_m" #> [10] "temperature_c" "salinity_psu" "chlorophyll_mg_m3" #> [13] "substrate" "abundance" "catch_weight_kg" #> [16] "present" "rare_species" ``` ::: ::: ## Python ```python import pandas as pd from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_raw raw = load_coastal_survey_raw() print(raw.shape) print(list(raw.columns)) ``` ::: Seventeen columns and 815 rows. So $n = 815$? ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tibble( `rows in the file` = nrow(raw), `after removing exact duplicates` = nrow(distinct(raw)), `distinct stations` = n_distinct(raw$station_id), `distinct sites` = n_distinct(raw$site_id) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| rows in the file| after removing exact duplicates| distinct stations| distinct sites| |----------------:|-------------------------------:|-----------------:|--------------:| | 815| 800| 800| 160|
::: ::: ## Python ```python pd.DataFrame({ "rows in the file": [len(raw)], "after removing exact duplicates": [len(raw.drop_duplicates())], "distinct stations": [raw["station_id"].nunique()], "distinct sites": [raw["site_id"].nunique()], }) ``` ::: Three different numbers, and the gap between the first and the last is a factor of five. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counts <- tibble( what = c("Rows in the file", "Unique rows", "Distinct stations", "Distinct sites"), n = c(nrow(raw), nrow(distinct(raw)), n_distinct(raw$station_id), n_distinct(raw$site_id)) ) |> mutate(what = fct_rev(fct_inorder(what))) ggplot(counts, aes(n, what)) + geom_col(fill = ml_palette[["blue"]], width = 0.62) + geom_text(aes(label = n), hjust = -0.2, size = 4) + scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) + labs(x = "Count", y = NULL, title = "How many observations is this?") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Four defensible answers to 'how many observations do I have?' from one file. Which is right depends on the question, but a model given the raw table will assume the first.](observations-and-features_files/figure-html/fig-what-is-n-1.png){#fig-what-is-n fig-alt='Horizontal bar chart with four bars: rows in the file, 815; unique rows, 800; distinct stations, 800; distinct monitoring sites, 160. The final bar is dramatically shorter than the others.' width=1400} ::: ::: Why so few sites? Because the survey revisits fixed stations. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} raw |> count(site_id, name = "visits") |> count(visits, name = "number_of_sites") |> arrange(visits) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| visits| number_of_sites| |------:|---------------:| | 1| 1| | 2| 13| | 3| 24| | 4| 34| | 5| 34| | 6| 15| | 7| 17| | 8| 11| | 9| 5| | 10| 3| | 11| 1| | 12| 1| | 15| 1|
::: ::: ## Python ```python (raw["site_id"].value_counts() .rename("visits") .value_counts() .rename("number_of_sites") .sort_index() .reset_index()) ``` ::: Most sites appear four to six times; one appears fifteen times. ## Counting the independent rows Fit a model on this table and it will treat all 815 rows as independent evidence. They are not, in three separate ways. **Fifteen rows are exact duplicates**: the same station entered twice. They add no information at all, but they add weight: a duplicated station counts double in the fitting, and, worse, can land in the training set *and* the test set at once, where it guarantees a perfect prediction it did not earn. That is leakage, and it has [its own page](information-leakage.qmd). **Stations at the same site are not independent of each other.** They are metres to hundreds of metres apart, in the same water, on the same substrate, often on the same day. Statistically they are closer to one observation with replicates than to five observations. This is pseudo-replication, and ecologists have been warning about it for decades; machine learning simply gives you faster ways to commit it. **Even across sites, nearby is not independent.** Two sites ten kilometres apart share water mass, depth and season. [Section 6](../06-assumptions-limitations/index.qmd) takes this seriously. The practical consequence is that **your effective sample size is nearer 160 than 815**, and every performance figure computed as though it were 815 will be optimistic. Not by a rounding error, but typically by a lot. Note what this does *not* mean. You should not throw away rows. The extra visits carry real information about within-site variation. What you must do is stop the *resampling* scheme from splitting a site across training and test data, which [section 7](../07-validation/index.qmd) handles with grouped resampling. The fix lives in how you validate, not in how much data you keep. ## Limits of the rectangle **Rectangles lose structure.** Flattening a depth profile into one row per cast throws away the shape of the profile; keeping one row per depth bin multiplies non-independent rows. Neither is free. The [next page](marine-data-types.qmd) deals with this. **The database schema is not a scientific decision.** Your data arrives at whatever granularity the survey software wrote it. That choice was made for data entry, not for your question, and it should not be adopted by default. **"Independent" is a property of the question, not the file.** Two trawls at one site are nearly the same observation for a habitat model, and two distinct observations for a model of gear variability. You cannot answer it by looking at the data alone. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Key points - Observation, feature, response, label: learn the synonyms, because the literature will use all of them. - Deciding what one row represents is a scientific decision, not a data-entry one. - The row count is not the sample size. Here: 815 rows, 800 unique, 160 sites. - Repeat visits, duplicate rows and spatial proximity all make rows share information. A model handed the raw table assumes none of that. - The fix is in the resampling scheme, not in deleting data: keep the rows, and keep a site's rows together. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Which site appears fifteen times? Look at its rows. How different are they from one another, compared with two rows drawn from different sites? 2. For your own data, write one sentence defining an observation, and one sentence naming what makes two of your rows non-independent. Almost every later decision in this course follows from those two sentences.
